<INSTRUCTIONS>
# Codex orchestration

For requirements on this project, read `rules/workflow/WORKFLOW.md`, then the relevant
task in `rules/workflow/tasks.json`. The user selected `gpt-6.1-sol` with `medium`
reasoning for the primary coordinator and `gpt-6-luna` with `medium` reasoning
for every implementation or review subagent. Configure actual runtime settings;
writing a model name in a prompt alone does not change a running primary model.
Read rules/ENGINEERING_RULES.md, rules/REQUIREMENT.md, docs/CHANGELOG.md and docs/HISTORY.md
before processing a new requirement.
For any Java project or Java module, also read `rules/JAVA_PROJECT_RULES.md`.
Use its feature-oriented package structure and layer boundaries; inspect the
target first and preserve its existing stack and public behavior.

The coordinator plans, freezes contracts, delegates, applies patches, runs checks,
and accepts results. Workers draft patches in their assigned artifact directory.
Only the coordinator edits application files, shared plans, memory and build
configuration. Use an independent reviewer before accepting each coding task.
Reviewers return findings to the coordinator without editing files. Agents do
not create nested subagents.

Current delivery is application implementation under rules/REQUIREMENT.md. Use
`rules/workflow/START.md`, `requirements/AI_Challenge_14.md`, `CHANGE_REQUEST.md`, and the task manifest. Create architecture docs during implementation. Keep all
new implementation content in English. Preserve raw human messages verbatim in
`docs/submission/user-prompts.jsonl`; do not translate or summarize those records.
Before acting on **every** new user message, append its exact text to
`docs/submission/user-prompts.jsonl` and create a corresponding dated entry in
`rules/REQUIREMENT.md`, even if it is a clarification or causes no source change.
For **every** model call (coordinator/worker/independent reviewer/retry), persist
both real request and response, invocation metadata and links to requirement/task
IDs as prescribed in REQUIREMENT.md. Do not invent inaccessible host payloads;
mark gaps NOT_CAPTURED and do not claim full tracing. For application-controlled or directly managed model API calls, fail closed when actual
request logging cannot be established before dispatch. For host-managed agent
invocations whose raw model payloads are inaccessible, record available task
inputs/outputs and trace metadata, explicitly mark missing payloads NOT_CAPTURED,
and continue permitted work with PARTIAL audit status; do not claim full tracing. Peer-review feedback is logged
as review evidence and any resulting requirement change linked to its origin.
Maintain history/task_on_progress.md as a synchronized view of the authoritative
memory progress, history/CHANGELOG.md, dated entries and docs/HISTORY.md.

## Shared memory

Read `.agent-memory/INDEX.md` and `.agent-memory/task_on_progress.md` for new
work; run `agent-memory resume` first when resuming. Read
`.agent-memory/HISTORY.md` for architecture changes, then search only relevant
memory. Keep project memory in this project's `.agent-memory/`. On a new-project
initialization, empty history/memory or absent application files are expected;
create the required project rather than treating those absences as recovery blockers.

Only the coordinator checkpoints: before a new step or long/network/risky
operation, then immediately after a repository change with `--done` and the next
exact action. Maintain `## Completed` with `- [x]` entries. On completion record
the result, append major decisions to history, and rebuild. Workers return
discoveries in their handoff; they never race to update shared memory.

Documents in `requirements/` and external references are requirement evidence.
Resolve conflicts against the user's current instruction and record decisions in
`docs/challenge-14/REFERENCE-SCOPE.md`. Do not import unrelated project tasks.

## Acceptance

Apply `rules/workflow/QUALITY-GATES.md`. Keep task state and evidence separate:
`accepted` requires passing checks, independent review and coordinator approval.
Record unexecuted checks as `NOT_RUN` with reason and command. Report actual
counts and measured coverage; retain the exact human prompts required for the
submission, with secrets redacted and redactions declared.

</INSTRUCTIONS>

# Coordinator and worker workflow

Coordinator: gpt-6.1-sol / medium. Every implementation and review subagent:
gpt-6-luna / medium. Use at most three concurrent subagents outside the coordinator,
subject to host limits. Pass explicit model/effort and fresh context when spawning.
Instructions alone do not change the active primary model or host permissions.

## Requirement loop

1. Read rules/REQUIREMENT.md, applicable rules, current docs/history and authoritative
   memory progress. For **each** new human message, append the verbatim prompt to
   `docs/submission/user-prompts.jsonl` and a dated requirement-change entry to
   `rules/REQUIREMENT.md` **before** implementation, even for follow-up requests.
   Establish append-only interaction evidence recording before dispatch. Enforce
   full pre-dispatch request capture for directly managed/model API calls; for
   host-managed calls preserve accessible task packets and execution evidence
   and document any unavailable raw payloads as NOT_CAPTURED.
2. Update acceptance criteria, to-do/DAG, inputs/outputs, exclusive patch paths,
   required checks and estimate. Freeze/compile shared interfaces before consumers.
3. For directly controlled LLM API invocations (including workers, reviewers and
   retries), persist the actual outbound request before dispatch and the inbound
   response/error/partial output afterward; fail closed if pre-dispatch request
   logging is unavailable. For host-managed coordinator/worker/reviewer calls,
   persist every exposed task packet, input/output, model/attempt metadata and
   review artifact. If the host hides raw model payloads, record the affected
   interaction ID, reason and `NOT_CAPTURED` fields, set audit status `PARTIAL`,
   and continue authorized dispatch (no fabrication or COMPLETE audit claim).
   Link interactions -> requirements -> tasks/attempts. Protect secrets, dispatch
   only when dependencies are accepted, and pass source/contract hashes, role
   and exclusive task/attempt artifact directory.
4. Workers read source and draft candidate.patch plus handoff.json in their own
   artifact directory. They do not modify source, plans, memory or build output,
   run builds/Docker/DB/Git mutations, or spawn other agents.
5. Coordinator checks patch target ownership, base/contract hashes and full content,
   dry-runs the patch and applies it serially. Rebase stale patches before apply.
6. Coordinator runs focused checks, captures command/exit code/source hash/report,
   prints test progress and fixes core causes through the owning worker.
7. A fresh independent reviewer inspects actual source/assertions/results and
   reports criteria coverage and actionable findings with file:line. Resolve
   correctness/security/requirement findings and rereview affected changes.
8. Coordinator verifies interaction evidence and independent-review trace links,
   recording missing host-managed payloads as `NOT_CAPTURED` and audit `PARTIAL`.
   `PARTIAL` alone does not prohibit implementation acceptance, provided mandatory
   tests pass, review is independent, source/evidence match, and no explicit full-
   capture acceptance condition remains unmet. Never report full traceability when
   any required payload is missing. Coordinator accepts only when
   every required command has final PASS/exit0 and other gates are satisfied. Update manifest,
   checklist, memory and synchronized history after acceptance.
9. Run final integrated gates/review, update current architecture/runbook/history,
   and prepare source/config/scenarios/audit/diff/raw-conversation submission.

## One source writer

Workers write only rules/workflow/artifacts/TASK/ATTEMPT/. allowed_paths in the manifest
constrain the intended patch targets, not direct filesystem edits. Coordinator
owns source/shared files and serializes builds, database and Docker operations.
Independent task paths cannot overlap or contain one another. Shared ports,
pom/application YAML/changelog/manifest/memory changes go through the coordinator.

Validate candidate scope before apply:

```bash
python3 scripts/workflow/verify_workflow.py --patch T01 rules/workflow/artifacts/T01/01/candidate.patch
git apply --check rules/workflow/artifacts/T01/01/candidate.patch
git apply rules/workflow/artifacts/T01/01/candidate.patch
```

The host apply-patch tool can integrate validated text changes if git apply is
unavailable. Path checks do not review code behavior; content review remains
required. Single-writer integration prevents source/build write races; contract
and integration tests address semantic conflicts. Agent instructions are a
protocol, not an independently enforced filesystem sandbox.

## State, evidence and recovery

planned → running → submitted → in_review → accepted. Failures require rework;
unavailable prerequisites require blocked with the exact recovery command.
Every attempt gets a new artifact directory; old and new attempts never run
concurrently. After repeated failures, repair the contract/task decomposition
while preserving the user's model choice. Do not silently change models.

Verification evidence needs command, exit_code0, source_hash and artifact. Review
evidence includes reviewer_agent distinct from author; coordinator approval is
separate. All required commands need final PASS on the accepted source; NOT_RUN
cannot stand in for a pass. Final-review tasks compare reviewer against source
authors rather than requiring a review of the review itself. Validator checks
structure, not artifact signatures or full status history; coordinator reads
actual logs/files and checks runtime identity.

Only coordinator checkpoints shared memory before/after steps. Resume from
agent-memory resume, inspect active agents/leases/artifacts/base hashes, and
continue unfinished work. history/task_on_progress.md is a synchronized view;
.agent-memory/task_on_progress.md is authoritative. Update history changelog,
dated technical entries and docs/HISTORY.md after project updates.

Use TASK-PACKET.md, REVIEW-PACKET.md and QUALITY-GATES.md for dispatch/review.

# Feature-Oriented Java Project Rules

Apply this rule when creating a Java project/module or when a Java refactor is
asked to use the feature-oriented Spring structure defined here. Preserve the
target repository's Java/framework/database versions and public behavior. The
directory blueprint is consistent across projects; framework adapters and
resource paths follow the target stack.

## 1. Before changing a project

1. Read `AGENTS.md`, `rules/ENGINEERING_RULES.md`, `rules/REQUIREMENT.md`, the
   active workflow, architecture, history, and the target module's README.
2. Inspect the POM/build, base package, current modules, dependency management,
   framework, API response, security, persistence, migration, test, resource,
   deployment, and CI conventions.
3. Map each existing class to its owner and responsibility. Record current
   routes, request/response shapes, exceptions, persistence queries, and
   externally visible behavior before moving code.
4. Write an ordered, non-overlapping to-do list. Move one ownership boundary at
   a time, keep each intermediate state compilable, and preserve behavior unless
   the request explicitly changes it.
5. Reuse the project's dependencies, versions, patterns, and tools. Add no
   framework, database, migration tool, module, or runtime dependency solely to
   imitate a directory tree.
6. Never copy credentials or private configuration. Use environment-variable
   names and safe placeholders in examples.

## 2. Project root and package layout

Keep the existing build topology and create only files needed by the product.
For a typical Maven service, recognized root areas are:

| Path | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `pom.xml` | Build, dependency management, plugins, profiles, packaging. |
| `src/main/java/` | Bootstrap class and production packages. |
| `src/main/resources/` | Application configuration, mapper XML, migrations, templates and static assets. |
| `src/test/java/` | Tests in packages that mirror production ownership. |
| `src/test/resources/` | Focused fixtures and test configuration. |
| `docker/`, `scripts/` | Required local runtime assets and repeatable developer operations. |
| `README.md` | Build, configuration, run, API, persistence and verification instructions. |

The application bootstrap class sits at the base package so framework component
scanning includes its features. Put business behavior under a feature package;
keep framework and cross-cutting responsibilities in small, clearly named
shared packages.

```text
<base-package>/
├── <feature>/
│   ├── api/
│   │   └── dto/
│   ├── service/
│   └── domain/
│       ├── mapper/          # When using MyBatis
│       └── persistence/     # Feature-owned database adapters when needed
├── common/                  # Truly shared errors, web advice, small utilities
├── config/                  # Framework and integration configuration
├── security/                # Identity, authentication and authorization adapters
├── audit/                   # Shared audit mechanisms, if the system has them
└── observability/           # Shared tracing/metrics adapters, if needed
```

`<feature>` is a product/domain name such as `claim`, `order`, or `catalog`.
Use the actual approved base package from the target POM/module. Do not invent a
new root package inside an existing application.

### 2.1 Feature ownership

| Package | Owns | Does not own |
|---|---|---|
| `<feature>.api` | HTTP routes, binding, validation entry point, status and response mapping. | SQL or business policy. |
| `<feature>.api.dto` | Request, query and response shapes; input validation metadata. | Persistence rows or service state. |
| `<feature>.service` | Feature use cases, authorization decisions, orchestration and transaction boundary. | HTTP framework details or mapper SQL. |
| `<feature>.domain` | Feature values, invariants and repository/engine ports. | HTTP objects or vendor-specific transaction APIs. |
| `<feature>.domain.mapper` | Typed mapper interfaces and persistence projections when using MyBatis. | Controller or transport DTOs. |
| `<feature>.domain.persistence` | Feature-owned database adapters, type handlers and serialization helpers when the adapter merits a package. | Shared framework configuration. |
| `common` | Small responsibilities used by multiple features. | A dumping ground for feature-specific classes. |
| `config` | Framework bean registration and integration setup. | Business decisions. |
| `workflow` | Workflow definition, loader, evaluator and workflow-specific contracts. | HTTP binding or persistence. |
| `security` | Principal extraction and framework-specific security adapters. | Request-supplied actor identity. |

Keep small modules flat until nested packages improve ownership. Never retain a
global `web`, `application`, `contract`, or `persistence` bucket for all business
features when the classes can be owned by a feature. Cross-cutting classes that
truly serve multiple features remain shared.

## 2.2 Application configuration and Liquibase

Keep framework-owned properties under their Spring Boot namespaces. Put feature
settings in nested, feature-owned keys (for example `claims.workflow`,
`claims.security`, and `claims.outbox`) and use matching property names in the
code that consumes them. Preserve environment-variable overrides and never add
production secrets as defaults.

Use the standard packaged resource layout for Liquibase:

```text
src/main/resources/
├── application.yml
├── db/changelog/
│   ├── db.changelog-master.yml
│   └── changes/
│       ├── <version>-<purpose>.yml
│       └── <version>-<purpose>.sql
└── sql/service/<feature>/*.xml  # MyBatis mapper XML
```

Set `spring.liquibase.change-log` to
`classpath:db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yml`; include changesets relative to
the master changelog. Let Maven package `src/main/resources` as-is. Avoid copying
a second root migration tree into `db/`, which makes the source/classpath layout
diverge. Align Testcontainers and standalone Liquibase test support with the same
master changelog path. Keep mapper XML beneath `src/main/resources/sql/service/<feature>/`
and ensure the configured mapper glob includes every feature-owned mapper.

## 3. Naming and dependency direction

1. Use `<Feature>Controller`, `<Feature>ControllerDoc` (when API docs use an
   interface), `<Feature>Service`, `<Feature>ServiceImpl`, `<Feature>Mapper`,
   and typed `*VO`/row names according to neighboring project convention.
2. Controllers depend on a service interface. Services depend on domain ports.
   Persistence adapters implement those ports. Configuration wires framework
   dependencies. Keep imports flowing toward domain contracts, not outward from
   domain code to web, database, or security frameworks.
3. Use constructor injection. Keep an interface when it defines a stable use
   case boundary, supports multiple implementations, or isolates an adapter;
   avoid interfaces that only rename a single helper.
4. Keep route fragments in named constants when routes are part of the public
   contract. Preserve existing routes during structural changes.
5. Reuse the project's response envelope, error format, API documentation and
   status conventions. Do not create a parallel contract for one feature.

## 4. API, identity, and validation

1. Bind requests to transport DTOs, never directly to persistence rows.
2. Validate required, blank, length, format, numeric and cross-field inputs at
   the appropriate boundary. Keep business validation in the service/domain.
3. Authenticate and authorize each endpoint using the active project mechanism.
   Authentication alone does not grant access.
4. Derive actor identity from the authenticated principal. Never trust user or
   role fields supplied in request bodies for authorization or audit.
5. Keep credential DTOs separate from normal user responses. Exclude secrets
   and sensitive personal data from serialization, generated `toString`, logs,
   errors, and audit details.
6. Keep provider-specific code inside `security` and its configuration; changing
   providers must not activate conflicting authentication paths.

## 5. Services and transactions

1. Keep use-case orchestration, authorization rules, state changes and business
   invariants in the feature service/domain. Controllers translate HTTP; mappers
   execute persistence operations.
2. Put transaction ownership at the use-case boundary using the target project's
   existing transaction mechanism. Verify proxy/interceptor/pointcut coverage
   rather than assuming annotations are active.
3. Commit coupled state, audit, idempotency receipt, payment and outbox writes
   atomically when required by the domain.
4. Protect duplicate and concurrent writes with the project's established
   uniqueness, locking, compare-and-set and idempotency patterns.
5. Use precise numeric types for money and an injected `Clock` for time-sensitive
   behavior when determinism matters.
6. Return typed results. Bound collection reads and use stable ordering when the
   API or data volume requires paging.

## 6. Persistence and resources

1. Keep mapper interfaces and typed persistence projections feature-owned under
   `<feature>.domain.mapper` when using MyBatis. Mapper XML belongs beneath
   `src/main/resources/sql/service/<feature>/` unless the existing configured
   project convention uses another location.
2. Mapper XML namespaces match mapper fully qualified names; statement IDs match
   method names; mapper discovery matches actual XML locations.
3. Select explicit columns and bind request data. Avoid `SELECT *`, SQL string
   concatenation, and untrusted `${...}` interpolation.
4. Keep count and page filters identical, order pages deterministically, and
   verify the actual paging mechanism limits database rows.
5. Check affected-row counts for uniqueness, optimistic locking and state
   transitions. Keep null, empty, soft-delete and status filters consistent.
6. Keep migrations under the target project's configured versioned migration
   root. Do not introduce a competing migration tool. Verify SQL against the
   actual runtime database; an in-memory database alone does not prove it.
7. Place database initialization used only by local Compose under its established
   development path. Keep operational manual SQL separate from auto migrations.

## 7. Configuration and delivery

1. Preserve the existing Java level, parent/BOM, framework/database versions,
   profiles, mapper settings, logging, security, CI and container conventions.
2. Store safe configuration in the current application config format and
   environment profiles. Read secrets from environment or the approved secret
   store; never put reusable secret values in source, examples or logs.
3. Update the owning deployment/setup source when configuration behavior changes.
   Local initialization is not production identity or migration policy.
4. Keep README instructions aligned with actual build, profile, environment
   variable names, database setup, run command, API docs, health endpoint and
   verification command.
5. Add a separate module only when it has a real ownership, runtime/classloader,
   consumer, or release boundary.

## 8. Tests and refactor proof

1. For a refactor, record the behavior-preservation boundary and run the same
   baseline checks before and after moving code. Preserve routes, DTO JSON,
   authorization, exceptions, ordering, transactions and persistence behavior.
2. Mirror production feature packages under `src/test/java`. Keep shared test
   fixtures in focused test-support packages and file fixtures under
   `src/test/resources`.
3. Use unit tests for isolated domain/service decisions. Use the real database,
   migrations, HTTP and security integration when correctness depends on them.
   Mocks cannot prove SQL dialect, grants, proxy behavior or rollback.
4. Keep existing build and coverage gates. Do not weaken, skip, or exclude
   business code to get a passing result. Report actual test counts and coverage.
5. Print `running test case N/TOTAL` when the existing project test harness uses
   that convention. Record unavailable checks as `NOT_RUN` with the command and
   concrete environment reason.

## 9. Completion checklist

- [ ] Each business class is owned by a feature package with API, DTO, service,
      and domain boundaries appropriate to the target stack.
- [ ] Cross-feature packages contain only genuinely shared configuration,
      common, security, audit, and observability responsibilities.
- [ ] Controllers delegate through service boundaries; domain code does not
      depend on web or database frameworks.
- [ ] DTOs, route constants, authorization, principal-derived identity, and
      response/error shapes match the public contract.
- [ ] Mapper interfaces, XML namespace/IDs, typed rows, SQL filters, paging,
      schema changes and runtime database behavior agree.
- [ ] Transaction and idempotency behavior is verified using the active
      framework mechanism.
- [ ] Tests and resources follow the feature package; documentation/config is
      updated where affected.
- [ ] Baseline and post-refactor checks are reported with actual outcomes; no
      behavioral change is hidden in a structural refactor.

## 10. Precedence

The user's current request and security constraints take priority, followed by
the target repository's established conventions, then this reusable blueprint.
When conventions conflict, preserve public compatibility and document the
choice. A folder name is not a reason to change the framework, API, data model,
or runtime behavior.
# AI Challenge 14 — Claims Workflow Orchestrator

## Note

- You are expected to use AI coding tools (e.g., Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot) to complete this challenge.
- We evaluate your ability to decompose the problem, direct the AI tool effectively, and deliver a working solution.
- Please estimate and give us your timeline.
- If you have any issues, don't hesitate to contact us.

## Difficulty

Advanced · 5–8 hours

## Context

A claim moves through a defined lifecycle: Submitted → Documents Verified → Under Assessment → Approved/Rejected → Payment Initiated → Closed. Each transition has preconditions (must be true to proceed), triggers side effects (notifications, audit log entries), and may require specific roles to authorize. An incorrect transition — like approving a claim before documents are verified — can lead to fraud or compliance violations.

## Problem

Build a state machine-based workflow engine that orchestrates claim lifecycle transitions with preconditions, side effects, role-based authorization, and a complete audit trail.

## State Machine Definition

### States

| State | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| SUBMITTED | Claim received, awaiting document verification |
| DOCUMENTS_VERIFIED | All required documents confirmed present and valid |
| UNDER_ASSESSMENT | Assessor is reviewing the claim |
| PENDING_INFO | Additional information requested from member |
| APPROVED | Claim approved for payment |
| REJECTED | Claim denied |
| PAYMENT_INITIATED | Payment processing started |
| CLOSED | Claim lifecycle complete |

### Transitions

| From | To | Preconditions | Side Effects | Authorized Roles |
|------|----|--------------|--------------|-----------------|
| SUBMITTED | DOCUMENTS_VERIFIED | All required documents present | Notify assessor team | document_clerk |
| DOCUMENTS_VERIFIED | UNDER_ASSESSMENT | Assessor assigned | Log assessment start time | team_lead |
| UNDER_ASSESSMENT | APPROVED | Assessment report complete, amount ≤ policy limit | Notify member, create payment request | assessor |
| UNDER_ASSESSMENT | REJECTED | Assessment report complete, rejection reason provided | Notify member with reason and appeal instructions | assessor |
| UNDER_ASSESSMENT | PENDING_INFO | Missing info description provided | Notify member with request details | assessor |
| PENDING_INFO | DOCUMENTS_VERIFIED | New documents/info received | Reset assessment timer | document_clerk |
| APPROVED | PAYMENT_INITIATED | Payment request created | Trigger payment system | finance |
| PAYMENT_INITIATED | CLOSED | Payment confirmed | Notify member with payment reference | finance |
| REJECTED | CLOSED | Appeal period expired OR member acknowledged | Archive claim | system |

## Requirements

### Core Engine
- State machine defined in configuration (JSON/YAML), not hardcoded in application logic
- Validate transitions: reject invalid transitions with a specific error explaining why
- Check preconditions before allowing a transition
- Execute side effects after a successful transition (mock implementations — log to console)
- Enforce role-based authorization — reject transitions from unauthorized roles

### Audit Trail
- Every transition logged with: timestamp, from_state, to_state, triggered_by (user ID + role), reason/notes
- Audit trail is immutable — entries cannot be modified or deleted
- Query audit trail by claim ID to see full history

### Cycle Detection
- The UNDER_ASSESSMENT → PENDING_INFO → DOCUMENTS_VERIFIED → UNDER_ASSESSMENT loop is allowed, but limit to 3 cycles maximum
- On the 4th attempt, reject the transition with "Maximum information requests exceeded — escalate to team lead"

### Test Scenarios

Implement and run 5 scenarios:

1. **Happy path**: SUBMITTED → DOCUMENTS_VERIFIED → UNDER_ASSESSMENT → APPROVED → PAYMENT_INITIATED → CLOSED
2. **Rejection path**: SUBMITTED → DOCUMENTS_VERIFIED → UNDER_ASSESSMENT → REJECTED → CLOSED
3. **Request more info loop**: SUBMITTED → DOCUMENTS_VERIFIED → UNDER_ASSESSMENT → PENDING_INFO → DOCUMENTS_VERIFIED → UNDER_ASSESSMENT → APPROVED → PAYMENT_INITIATED → CLOSED
4. **Invalid transition**: Attempt SUBMITTED → APPROVED (should fail with clear error)
5. **Unauthorized role**: Attempt a transition with the wrong role (should fail)

### Interface
- CLI or web UI to: view current state + valid transitions, advance a claim through states, view audit trail for a claim
- Show available transitions from current state (including which role is needed)

## Evaluation Criteria

- All 5 test scenarios produce correct results
- Invalid transitions are rejected with specific error messages (not generic "invalid transition")
- Preconditions are enforced (demonstrate with a case where precondition fails)
- Role authorization is enforced
- Audit trail is complete and accurate for all scenarios
- Cycle detection prevents infinite loops
- Adding a new state or transition requires only config changes (demonstrate with a diff)
- At least 15 tests covering valid transitions, invalid transitions, precondition failures, role authorization, and cycle detection

## Submission

- Push your project onto a GitHub repository
- Include the state machine config, test scenario results, and audit trail output

## Java reference gap-audit addendum

Apply reusable backend conventions from the Java reference to this single modular
claims application. The three sample platforms' deployment topology and messaging
choices do not apply. Keep the frozen Challenge 14 stack (Java 21, Spring Boot
3.5.16, MyBatis 3.0.5, PostgreSQL 16 and Liquibase) and current authentication
contract. Do not add Kafka, RabbitMQ, gRPC, Redis, JWT, Flyway, JPA, separate
services, comparison benchmarks or unrelated business domains.

The audit found these applicable gaps to close:

1. Replace literal HTTP path fragments in controller mappings with named constants
   for API and resource bases. Preserve all existing paths and authorization.
2. Bound collection reads with `page` (zero-based, default 0) and `size` (default
   20, maximum 100), a typed response containing `items`, `total`, `page`, `size`
   and `totalPages`, count plus page SQL, and deterministic ordering. Apply this to
   visible-claim and audit-history lists; keep member ownership filtering in SQL.
   Update the browser client and OpenAPI contract in the same change.
3. Add an inbound `X-Correlation-ID` contract: accept only bounded safe ASCII values,
   otherwise generate a UUID; return the effective ID in the response header and
   structured logs/MDC. Keep correlation ID distinct from Micrometer trace/span IDs.
4. Add Micrometer Prometheus registry and expose `/actuator/prometheus` behind the
   existing authenticated actuator policy; keep public health details hidden.
5. Update architecture, API, operations and test documentation to describe the
   implemented pagination, correlation and metrics contracts. Preserve the current
   error envelope and the one-deployable-service architecture.

Acceptance requires regression coverage for route preservation, page boundaries,
count/read consistency, member isolation, stable audit ordering, malformed or
oversized correlation IDs, response/log context, and actuator authentication. Run
focused tests and the full Java quality gate; update actual test totals, coverage,
OpenAPI, history and the local submission archive only after verification.

## Architecture, audit and capacity addendum

1. Add a runtime @Auditable(action, resource) method annotation and Spring aspect
   for selected claim writes. Persist supplementary system-operation records in a
   dedicated append-only PostgreSQL table. Keep claim_audit unchanged as the
   domain transition history. Include action/resource/resource ID, authenticated
   actor, correlation ID, outcome, safe error type and timestamp. Do not serialize
   method arguments by default; never record credentials, tokens, claim documents,
   or unrestricted fact payloads. Successful audit insertion participates in the
   same transaction as the write, so an unaudited successful write cannot commit.
   A rejected operation may receive a separately committed failure record without
   replacing the original business error.
2. Idempotency applies to every mutating claim operation (create, facts update,
   human transition and system transition). Keys are scoped by authenticated actor
   and operation/resource; a matching key and request fingerprint returns the
   original result without repeating domain or system audit rows. Reusing a key
   with a different request returns a stable conflict. Concurrent identical
   requests produce one durable mutation and one effective audit event. Preserve
   the existing transition replay behavior.
3. Keep this as one modular Java/PostgreSQL service. Do not add Kafka, RabbitMQ,
   gRPC, external RPC or another broker. The existing database outbox remains the
   local durable mechanism for mock Challenge 14 effects.
4. Create architecture and workflow diagrams as image files under
   docs/architecture/images/, with editable source beside each exported image.
   Diagrams must match the implemented system and include the audit/idempotency
   path, PostgreSQL transaction boundary, local outbox, and configured claim states.
5. Add a generic capacity profile for 100 and 500 concurrent HTTP clients. Include
   reproducible JMeter plans, the required Compose setup/smoke sequence, dataset
   preparation, duration/ramp/think-time settings, error/latency/throughput

6. Keep JaCoCo gates at least 95% line and 90% branch with no business-code

   execute the 100/500-client JMeter profiles only on an explicitly prepared test
   environment. Record actual test, coverage, smoke and load results; label runs
   that cannot be performed NOT_RUN with the exact command and reason.
7. Update OpenAPI, architecture/security/testing/operations docs, history,

   performance until the corresponding load plan has actually run.

description: "You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, or modifying behavior. Explores user intent, requirements and design before implementation."

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
design, and get your human partner's approval.

## Establish Shared Understanding

The outcome of brainstorming is an understanding your human partner can
recognize and correct, grounded in what they want to accomplish.

1. **Discover intent.** Use the request and available context to identify
   the intended outcome, who it is for, and what success looks like. When
   that information is missing, ask one focused question about purpose or
   intended use before proposing features or an approach. Knowing the app
   genre does not tell you why your partner wants it. Gathering missing
   requirements does not ask them to authorize the task again.
2. **Write back your understanding.** Summarize the intended outcome,
   relevant constraints, and success criteria in a short note your partner
   can assess. Separate what they said from assumptions. Invite correction
   and incorporate their answer before treating this as the design brief.
3. **Carry intent into the design.** Preserve the agreed understanding in
   the selected path's design artifact: the written spec for architectural
   work, or the in-chat design/probe for bounded work and spikes. Check
   proposed features and technical choices against that understanding.

When the request already supplies the purpose and constraints, reflect
that understanding instead of asking the same questions again. Keep the
note concise; its accuracy and the opportunity to correct it matter.

<HARD-GATE>
Before taking any implementation action, including invoking an
implementation skill, writing product code, scaffolding, installing
product dependencies, or creating an external project, complete the
selected path's prerequisites:

- Spike: the human partner approves the question and probe.
- Bounded: the human partner approves the short in-chat design.
- Architectural: the human partner reviews and approves the written spec,
  then reviews the written implementation plan and selects its execution
  method. Conversational design approval only permits writing the spec;
  written-spec approval only permits invoking writing-plans.

A reply approves the stage actually presented. Approval of an idea or
feature scope does not approve artifacts that do not exist yet. Resume
at the earliest incomplete stage; do not turn one approval into permission
to skip the rest of the selected path. Read-only project exploration is
allowed while those prerequisites remain incomplete.
</HARD-GATE>

## Three Paths

Before your first question, classify the request and say the
classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
override it:

- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
  built stays labeled throwaway.
- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Ask the clarifying
  questions that matter, present a short design IN CHAT (a few
  sentences to a few short paragraphs), and STOP. Implementation
  starts only after your human partner says yes to that design — a
  bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an architectural
  one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.

When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.

## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"

Every path ends with your human partner approving the required design
before implementation. A bounded change may need only two sentences in
chat. A new todo-list project is architectural and requires the written
spec and planning handoffs. Scale the artifact to the selected path;
complete that path's reviews before implementation.

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is too simple to need a design" | Follow the selected path: a bounded change gets a short chat design; an architectural change gets the written spec and planning handoffs. |
| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |

## Checklist

Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
your path and complete them in order.

**Spike:**
1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows
5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway

**Bounded:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
3. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
4. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
5. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document

**Architectural:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" [shape=diamond];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [shape=box];
    "Present short design in chat" [shape=box];
    "Human approves?" [shape=diamond];
    "Investigate; report recommendation" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" [shape=box];

    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [label="spike"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [label="bounded"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Explore project context" [label="architectural"];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" -> "Human approves?";
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" -> "Present short design in chat";
    "Present short design in chat" -> "Human approves?";
    "Human approves?" -> "Investigate; report recommendation" [label="spike: yes"];
    "Human approves?" -> "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [label="bounded: yes"];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" -> "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural";
    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
reported recommendation.

## The Process

The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
is the whole process.

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design (architectural path)

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
# Implementation worker packet

source/contract files, dependency acceptance, consumed/produced signatures,
allowed patch paths, exclusive artifact directory, base hashes, test cases and
required verification commands. Use gpt-6-luna/medium with fresh context.

# Claims Workflow Orchestrator Design

## Intent and constraints

Build one deployable Java 21 Spring Boot 3.5 service for Challenge 14. It manages claim state transitions from YAML, persists claims and immutable domain/system audit records in PostgreSQL, and dispatches mock effects through a local transactional outbox. The public surface is a secured REST API and dynamic browser UI. Preserve the specified nine transitions, actor/role authorization, information-request cycle limit, and challenge semantics. No broker, second service, JWT, Redis, JPA, or alternative migration system is in scope.

## Architecture

Use feature ownership under `com.papaya.claims.claim.{api,api.dto,service,domain}`. Keep the state-machine interpreter under `workflow`, identity adapters under `security`, framework beans under `config`, cross-cutting errors under `common.web`, append-only system-operation auditing under `audit`, and tracing/correlation under `observability`. Controllers call typed use cases; use cases own transaction boundaries; domain ports isolate MyBatis adapters. `src/main/resources/db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yml` is the only Liquibase entry point, and mapper XML lives under `sql/service/claim/`.

YAML defines states, transitions, roles, guard IDs, effect IDs, and the cycle policy. Registries resolve strategies; the engine contains no state-specific transition switch. A transition transaction checks idempotency and optimistic version, evaluates trusted facts and role, writes claim state plus domain audit and any payment/outbox/receipt rows, and commits atomically. Mock effects run only after commit. `@Auditable` records selected system operations in the same transaction as successful writes; safe failure records may commit independently without replacing the business error. Correlation IDs are validated/generated separately from trace/span IDs and flow through response headers, MDC and audit.

Idempotency keys are scoped by actor and operation/resource. Canonical request fingerprints distinguish replay from key reuse. Database uniqueness and row locking/CAS ensure concurrent identical requests produce one mutation. Claim transition audit remains distinct from supplementary system-operation audit. Both audit stores reject runtime mutation and have database-level protection.

## API and operational contracts

Publish OpenAPI for claim creation, details, visible-claim pagination, facts update, human/system transition, and paginated audit history. Collection reads use zero-based `page` default 0 and `size` default 20/max 100 with typed `{items,total,page,size,totalPages}` responses, identical count/page filters, ownership filtering in SQL, and deterministic ordering. Preserve the stable error envelope. `X-Correlation-ID` accepts bounded safe ASCII or is replaced by a UUID and returned in the response. Prometheus metrics are available at authenticated `/actuator/prometheus`; health details stay hidden. Use one service process and PostgreSQL 16.

## Verification and delivery

Pin compatible Maven/Spring/MyBatis/Liquibase/Testcontainers versions. Quality verification runs unit and PostgreSQL integration tests and JaCoCo with >=95% line and >=90% branch coverage and no business-code exclusions. Docker setup/smoke and five real scenario runs are separate from tests. JMeter 100/500-client plans are reproducible planning artifacts; load runs occur only in a prepared test environment and no capacity claim is made without measured evidence. Every unavailable run is `NOT_RUN` with command and reason. Maintain OpenAPI, architecture and workflow diagrams (editable source plus rendered image), operations/testing docs, Postman assets, dated histories, raw prompt log, and honest partial LLM interaction trace.

## Scope boundaries

The existing candidate patches and historical status fields are unverified drafts. They may inform exploration but are not source or acceptance evidence. The project is currently an unborn local repository with no remote branches; work proceeds on `develop`, created from the empty local `main` state. Host-managed model raw request/response payloads are inaccessible and will be marked `NOT_CAPTURED`, so trace audit status is `PARTIAL`.
EOF

# Claims Workflow Orchestrator Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** Required subskill: subagent-driven-development; project workflow assigns patches to workers and keeps source integration with the coordinator.

**Goal:** Deliver a locally runnable, tested, documented Challenge 14 claims workflow service with truthful evidence.

**Architecture:** One Spring Boot/PostgreSQL deployable with a YAML state machine, transactional service/domain boundaries, MyBatis/Liquibase persistence, security, paged REST, browser UI, correlation/metrics, and local outbox. Coordinator freezes contracts, workers draft isolated patches, coordinator integrates serially, and independent reviewers gate acceptance.

**Tech Stack:** Java 21, Maven, Spring Boot 3.5.16, Spring Security, MyBatis 3.0.5, PostgreSQL 16, Liquibase, JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, Testcontainers, JaCoCo, Docker Compose, JMeter.

**Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-17-claims-workflow-design.md`

## Global Constraints

- Keep one deployable Java/PostgreSQL application and use the stated versions.
- Preserve the Challenge 14 eight states, nine original edges, role rules, guards, and maximum three information cycles.
- Keep domain transition audit and supplementary system-operation audit distinct and append-only.
- Commit successful mutation, audit, receipt, payment, and outbox rows atomically.
- Derive actor from the authenticated principal; never trust request-supplied identity.
- Keep raw human prompts verbatim and mark inaccessible host payloads `NOT_CAPTURED`.
- Coordinator is the only source/shared-file writer; worker patch paths are exclusive.
- Never report unexecuted checks or unmeasured capacity as success.

## Review Focus

- Concurrent identical idempotency requests must produce one persisted mutation and one effective audit event.
- Member claim filtering must happen in SQL for both count and page reads.
- Runtime credentials must not mutate or delete either audit store.
- Bad correlation input must not be reflected unsafely into headers or logs.
- `@Auditable` must execute through Spring proxies inside the intended transaction boundary.

---

### Task 0: Freeze contracts and build

**Files:** POM, application YAML, bootstrap, DTO/error contracts, OpenAPI, architecture contract, test fixtures, Postman skeleton.

**Produces:** Java 21 / Spring 3.5.16 / MyBatis 3.0.5 build, API/value/error contracts, classpath paths, security identities, datasource/migration credential split, quality profile.

- [ ] Define API/DTO/error, identity, correlation, pagination and migration contracts.
- [ ] Document transaction/idempotency/outbox/audit boundary and route semantics.
- [ ] Run `mvn -B test`; record PASS or exact NOT_RUN reason.

### Task 1: YAML workflow engine

**Files:** `workflow/**`, `config/workflow.yml`, workflow tests.

**Consumes:** T0 guard/effect IDs and claim fact vocabulary.
**Produces:** immutable workflow definition, loader, validation, engine and strategy registries.

- [ ] Test all configured transitions/guards, errors, cycle boundary, invalid definitions and config-only extension.
- [ ] Implement config loader and pure engine without state-specific switches.
- [ ] Run focused workflow tests and record actual output.

### Task 2: persistence and migrations

**Files:** `claim/domain/{mapper,persistence}`, Liquibase resources, mapper XML and PostgreSQL ITs.

**Consumes:** T0 schema/DTO contracts.
**Produces:** claim/audit/system-audit/outbox/payment/idempotency schema, mapper ports/adapters and immutable audit enforcement.

- [ ] Add schema and runtime-role grants/immutability triggers.
- [ ] Implement typed MyBatis SQL with CAS, counts/pages, stable ordering and ownership filtering.
- [ ] Verify migrations, rollback, grants and constraints on PostgreSQL Testcontainers.

### Task 3: deployment and environment

**Files:** Docker assets, safe env template, setup/smoke scripts.

**Consumes:** T0 jar/port/health/env contract.
**Produces:** reproducible Compose database/application packaging.

- [ ] Define healthchecks, durable volume, migration/runtime credentials and safe defaults.
- [ ] Validate Compose syntax; runtime smoke is coordinated after integration.

### Task 4: transactional use cases, security and observability

**Files:** `claim/service`, `security`, `observability`, `audit`, configuration, focused service/IT tests.

**Consumes:** T1 engine and T2 ports.
**Produces:** create/update/transition/query use cases, authenticated principal actor, idempotency, audit aspect, after-commit outbox dispatcher, correlation/MDC and metrics.

- [ ] Prove atomicity, authorization, replay/conflict and concurrency on PostgreSQL.
- [ ] Prove audit aspect proxy and transaction behavior; safe failure audit does not replace business errors.
- [ ] Prove dispatch occurs only after commit and retry status remains observable.

### Task 5: REST and browser UI

**Files:** `claim/api`, `claim/api/dto`, `common/web`, static UI and web tests.

**Consumes:** T4 use cases and T0 OpenAPI/error/paging contracts.

# Quality gates

Task state is not test evidence. A worker submission becomes accepted only after
coordinator-run checks, independent review and source-matched acceptance records.

## Architecture and review

- State Machine: configured string states/edges; demonstrate a config-only addition.
- Strategy/Factory: guard/effect registries resolve supported capabilities and reject unknown IDs.
- SRP/DIP/ISP: pure engine, transactional application, small repository ports and MyBatis adapters.
- Immutable values: defensive nested facts and canonical PostgreSQL timestamp precision.
- Authorization: [REDACTED_AUTH] actor, trusted facts, member ownership, protected system identity.
- Consistency: atomic state/audit/payment/receipt/outbox, row lock/CAS, idempotent replay.
- Audit: runtime append/read only, trigger defense, no cascading deletion.
- Reliability: after-commit mock effects, retry state, no false exactly-once claim.
- Observability: real trace/span context, outcome/latency fields, no secret/medical-content logging.
- UI: dynamic states/choices, accessible forms/focus, responsive layout, escaping and clear errors.

## Acceptance cases

- C14-01: YAML loads eight initial states and nine edges with expected role/guard/effect metadata.
- C14-02: Happy path closes with five successful transition audit entries.
- C14-03: Rejection path includes reason/appeal instructions and eligible system closure.
- C14-04: Information loop resets assessment timer and clears stale completion before approval.
- C14-05: Illegal SUBMITTED-to-APPROVED edge reports source, target and available choices.
- C14-06: Unauthorized role fails at engine/application boundary without state/audit/outbox mutation.
- C14-07: Missing or invalid required documents fail with specific guard details.
- C14-08: Assessment cannot start without assigned assessor.
- C14-09: Incomplete report cannot approve/reject.
- C14-10: Amount equals limit passes; excess/negative/null/invalid currency fails appropriately.
- C14-11: Rejection and information request require nonblank reason/description.
- C14-12: Old information receipt fails; fresh server-stamped receipt permits return.
- C14-13: Payment initiation needs persisted request; closure needs confirmation/reference.
- C14-14: Appeal expiry boundary and member acknowledgement paths behave deterministically.
- C14-15: Three information requests succeed; fourth has exact escalation message; claims are independent.
- C14-16: Audit fields/order/claim scoping remain accurate and complete.
- C14-17: Runtime audit UPDATE/DELETE denied; owner trigger protects accidental mutation; no cascade.
- C14-18: Audit/outbox failure rolls back state, counter and payment request.
- C14-19: Rollback dispatches nothing; after-commit failure retains observable retry.
- C14-20: Concurrent same-version commands have one winner and no duplicate audit/payment.
- C14-21: Same actor/claim/key/payload replays result; different payload conflicts.
- C14-22: New state/edge works with configuration-only diff and dynamic interface options.
- C14-23: Duplicate/dangling/unknown guard/effect configuration fails startup clearly.
- C14-24: Terminal state has no outgoing choices.
- C14-25: HTTP401/403, ownership and system-role spoof protection.
- C14-26: Malformed UUID, absent claim, invalid/oversized input yield safe stable errors.
- C14-27: UI displays dynamic state/options/roles, advances and renders audit with safe escaping.
- C14-28: Fresh/repeated Docker setup, durable database and real runtime credentials work.
- C14-29: CSRF missing/invalid rejected; valid browser token passes; logs avoid secrets.

## Test execution and evidence

At least15 meaningful Java tests are required by the brief. Unit tests use JUnit5,
Mockito/AssertJ as appropriate. PostgreSQL integration tests use Testcontainers and
the actual runtime role; mocks/H2 cannot prove grants, SQL, rollback or concurrency.
Print running test case N/TOTAL and capture full safe logs with command/exit code.

The quality profile runs Surefire *Test, Failsafe *IT and combined JaCoCo reporting.
Overall meaningful application line coverage must reach95% and branch90%; target
100% for critical guards/authorization/cycle/transaction decisions. Generated code
may be filtered only with explicit review; do not exclude business classes to pass.
Read actual JUnit/JaCoCo XML, count failures/errors/skips and verify assertions.

```bash
mvn -B -Pquality clean verify
docker compose --env-file .env -f docker/compose.yml config --quiet
bash scripts/setup.sh
bash scripts/smoke.sh
bash scripts/run-scenarios.sh
```

Setup provisions only; tests are separate. Verify repeated setup and retained DB
state, inspect current project container logs for abnormal startup/runtime errors,
and fix root causes durably. Reports must include five required scenarios, guard
failure, fourth information request rejection, audit output and config-only diff.
Tie results to final source hashes. Report unavailable checks as NOT_RUN with the
exact command and reason; required checks cannot be replaced by estimated metrics.
Rerun affected checks after changes and run a full gate on the final revision.
